prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Document: Management by Trajectory (MBT) concept for future air traffic management (ATM) in the National Airspace System (NAS). MBT is one specific interpretation of the high-level Trajectory Based Operations (TBO) vision (4D contract), consistent with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) TBO Concept Document. Current NAS: ATM automation predicts trajectories from flight plan plus departure time; controllers tactically issue 'open trajectory' vectors, altitude and speed clearances not communicated to automation or stakeholders, degrading demand prediction. Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) and Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) assign departure times to meet a Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA); Time Based Flow Management (TBFM) assumes estimated times of arrival (ETAs) are correct; Traffic Flow Management (TFM) reroutes are left to controllers. MBT: the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and airspace users (commercial, Unmanned Aircraft Systems, space vehicles, on-demand air transportation) negotiate four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs) for all flights. Assigned 4DTs respect all known constraints to destination; NAS constraint impacts are inserted as trajectory constraints, with proactive modifications as early as possible. Pilots and controllers use automation to keep aircraft on trajectory; equipped aircraft are substantially responsible for compliance. Enablers: ground and aircraft automation, air-ground and ground-ground data communications. Shortfalls and MBT improvements (Table 1): sparse user-FAA data exchange -> data for accurate, consistent 4DT predictions available to all airspace users, aircraft and FAA automation systems; open trajectories -> aircraft operate on closed trajectories where possible; poor publication/synchronization -> all trajectory changes published and trajectory information exchanged in advance between ground automation and aircraft for trajectory synchronization; poor predictability inhibits strategic management -> controllers use strategic, closed clearances; high predictability is the norm, improving TFM so demand matches capacity, reducing delay; all dynamic (e.g., TFM) and static (e.g., crossing restrictions) NAS constraints are published to all airspace users and relevant automation systems. Actors: FAA, airspace users, pilots, controllers, ATM/ground automation, aircraft automation, other stakeholders.

New part:
U0042: All constraints affecting a given aircraft are reflected in the 4DT.
U0043: Lack of knowledge about certain types of constraints prevents airspace users from planning business-efficient, acceptable trajectories.
U0044: Those constraints also are unknown to every ground automation system, causing aircraft to be handled with an open- ended clearance when the constraints are encountered.
U0045: Insufficient mechanisms to allow traffic managers and controllers to efficiently and effectively amend flights’ routes cause route amendment backlogs during disruptive NAS events.
U0046: Traffic managers apply constraints to efficiently amend trajectories as NAS events evolve, enabling a more flexible and responsive ATM system that can take full advantage of available airspace and drastically reduce delay.2 There is not a good mechanism that allows controllers and traffic managers to predict the downstream consequences of an action or decision on specific aircrafts’ trajectories.
U0047: Downstream effects of actions on a trajectory are considered in decision making associated with a given trajectory, including tactical control actions.
U0048: By quantifying time-based performance as a metric that complements existing PBN metrics, all IFR aircraft may be managed by a single ATM concept that maximizes efficiency while maintaining an acceptable level of safety risk.
U0049: Current time of arrival control (TOAC) standards establish a minimum performance requirement that some aircraft will be certified for while others will not.
U0050: This type of standard may inadvertently introduce unacceptable safety risk into the NAS and creates a mixed equipage environment in which one ATM concept applies to those who meet the standard while another concept must be applied to those who do not. 1.2 MBT Overview The MBT concept can be summarized by the following key points.  MBT applies to all aircraft operating according to Instrument Flight Rules (IFR).  Aircraft are assigned 4DTs, which are negotiated, closed trajectories, from their current state to their destination.  A NAS Constraint Service publishes common information about NAS constraints to all stakeholders.  Trajectory constraints can be mapped to NAS constraints to facilitate identifying affected aircraft when NAS constraints change.  All aircraft follow their negotiated, assigned trajectories, complying with trajectory constraints.  Trajectory constraints and associated tolerances are defined based on the flight’s individual performance capabilities and the situational need for the constraint. 2 This document does not describe the details of how traffic managers or traffic management automation determines what trajectory constraints to impose on each flight.
